claims.statement: Cancer comprises diseases in which abnormal cells grow without normal control and can invade nearby tissue. Many cancers form solid tumors; blood cancers need not form a solid mass.
limitations: Tumor behavior, lineage, stage, and molecular features vary among cancers.

claims.statement: Metastasis is spread from the original cancer site to another part of the body. Metastatic breast cancer in the lung is classified as breast cancer that has spread, rather than a new primary lung cancer.
limitations: A person can also develop a separate primary cancer; site alone does not establish lineage.

claims.statement: Cancer involves genetic changes, but genetic does not mean inherited. Changes can arise during cell division or after environmental exposures, as well as being inherited.
limitations: An inherited susceptibility variant changes risk; it does not imply that every carrier will develop cancer.

claims.statement: Cancer cells can differ between people, between regions of a tumor, and over time as further changes occur. A biomarker test samples a particular specimen at a particular time.
limitations: A single specimen may not represent every cancer cell or a later disease state.

claims.statement: Changes in growth-control, tumor-suppressor, and DNA-repair genes can contribute to cancer development. Finding a variant in a tumor does not by itself establish that it drives growth or predicts response to a treatment.
limitations: Variants can be benign or of unknown significance; causal and treatment claims need additional evidence.

claims.statement: Tumor biomarker testing can inform treatment research and selection. It differs from testing specifically intended to identify inherited cancer susceptibility; a possible inherited finding in a tumor may need confirmation with an appropriate germline test.
claims.population: Distinguishing somatic and inherited molecular information
limitations: Tumor testing can incidentally suggest an inherited change; its presence alone does not establish family members' genetic status.

claims.statement: Biomarkers include genes, proteins, and other measurable features. Some inform treatment selection, but a matching marker does not guarantee benefit because other biological features, cell mixtures, and changes over time affect response.
limitations: Actionability depends on the exact alteration, cancer context, test performance, and evidence for the proposed use.

claims.statement: A prognostic use concerns likely disease course or outcome; a predictive use concerns response to a particular intervention. A marker associated with poor outcomes is not automatically evidence that one treatment works better for marker-positive patients.
claims.population: Interpretation of biomarker context of use
limitations: One biomarker can have different roles in different contexts; the clinical question and supporting comparison must be stated.

claims.statement: Early cancer trial phases emphasize safety and initial activity, while phase 3 studies compare an intervention with a relevant standard. Eligibility criteria and randomized assignment address different design questions: who is studied and how comparison groups are formed.
limitations: Phase is a design label, not a guarantee of benefit; results depend on the actual population, comparator, endpoints, and analysis.

claims.topic: objective response, progression-free survival, and overall survival
claims.statement: Objective response measures predefined tumor shrinkage. Progression-free survival measures time until progression or death under the trial's definitions. Overall survival measures time until death from any cause. A change in one endpoint does not automatically establish a change in the others.
limitations: Definitions, assessment schedules, censoring, duration of response, and disease context matter; these endpoints should not be pooled as interchangeable measures.
